text: Charts do not lie by themselves, but they're easy to make misleading, sometimes on purpose and more often by accident. As a data scientist you have two jobs: spot these tricks when you read other people's charts, and never commit them in your own.

Average spend by region: South two hundred eighty-three, West three hundred twenty-five, about fifteen percent higher. Start the y-axis at two hundred eighty instead of zero, and the South bar is only three units tall while West is forty-five, so West looks fifteen times taller. The real ratio is one point one five. Bars encode value by length, so a bar chart must start at zero.

Line charts encode position and slope, so they may zoom to a non-zero range, as long as the axis is clearly labeled. But two series on two separate y-axes can be made to look tightly linked or totally unrelated just by choosing each axis range, without changing a single data point.

Cherry-picked windows tell a different story from the same data. Our illustrative revenue rose forty-six percent over the full year, but one two-month slice, August to September, shows a three point nine percent dip. Show only those two months and the headline becomes revenue is falling. Always show enough history that the reader can judge the trend.

Distorted shapes mislead too. Three D bars and pies tilt shapes so front elements look bigger. Exploded pie slices distort angle comparisons. And if a bubble's radius scales with the value, its area grows with the square, so a value twice as big looks four times as big. Scale area, not radius.

Quieter tricks: missing labels or units so nobody can check the numbers, sorting that hides an inconvenient category, a cut-off axis with no marker saying so, and showing a correlation as if it proved a cause.

Before you publish any chart, run the honesty checklist: zero baseline, one honest y-axis, the full time range, flat shapes scaled by area, complete labels, and a chart that still makes sense next to the raw numbers. Next: we move into Python and matplotlib fundamentals.
